# Environment variables on Windows 11

Environment variables are pieces of named text the operating system
makes available to every program — for example `%TEMP%` (the user's
temporary folder) or `%PATH%` (where Windows looks for command-line
programs).

## Opening the Environment Variables editor

1. Press **Windows key + R**, type `sysdm.cpl`, press **Enter**.
2. Click the **Advanced** tab.
3. Click **Environment Variables…** at the bottom.

There are two lists:

* **User variables** — apply only to the signed-in user.
* **System variables** — apply to all users on this computer.

## Adding a folder to PATH

`PATH` is a semicolon-separated list of folders. Programs in any of
those folders can be run by name from the command line.

1. In the editor, select **Path** under **User variables**.
2. Click **Edit**.
3. Click **New** and type the folder path, for example
   `C:\Tools\bin`.
4. Click **OK** to close all three dialogs.
5. Open a new terminal window — old terminals still see the old PATH.

## Setting a variable from PowerShell

```
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("MY_VAR", "value", "User")
```

The third argument is `User` or `Machine`. Open a new terminal to see
the new value.

## Common built-in variables

* `%USERPROFILE%` — your home folder, like `C:\Users\Jane`.
* `%APPDATA%` — `C:\Users\Jane\AppData\Roaming`.
* `%LOCALAPPDATA%` — `C:\Users\Jane\AppData\Local`.
* `%TEMP%` — your temporary files folder.
* `%PROGRAMFILES%` — `C:\Program Files`.

## Reverting a bad change

If you accidentally erased PATH and important programs stopped
working, sign out and back in — Windows applies fresh defaults from
the registry. If a system PATH was wiped, restore from a System
Restore point made before your change.

# Set default apps on Windows 11

Windows opens files with the **default app** for that file type — for
example, .pdf files open in Edge by default. You can change this to
any installed app.

## Change the default browser

1. Open **Settings → Apps → Default apps**.
2. Type your preferred browser (Chrome, Firefox, etc.) into the
   search box.
3. Click the browser when it appears.
4. Click **Set default** at the top right of its detail page.

This changes the default for HTTP, HTTPS, and HTML.

## Change the default app for a specific file type

1. **Settings → Apps → Default apps**.
2. Scroll down and click **Choose defaults by file type**.
3. Find the extension (like `.pdf`) and click the current default.
4. Pick the app you want.

## Change defaults from File Explorer

1. Right-click any file with the type you want to change.
2. Choose **Open with → Choose another app**.
3. Pick the app and check **Always use this app to open .xxx files**.
4. Click **OK**.

## Reset defaults

If apps got jumbled and you want to start over:

1. **Settings → Apps → Default apps**.
2. Scroll to **Reset all default apps** and click **Reset**.

## Why "Set default" sometimes does not work

If an app does not stick as default, the app may not be properly
registered with Windows. Reinstall it and try again. Microsoft Edge
also resets some defaults during major Windows updates — Windows asks
before doing this.

# Virtual desktops and Task View on Windows 11

Virtual desktops let you have several "screens" of open apps without
needing more monitors — for example a desktop for personal browsing
and another for video calls.

## Opening Task View

* Click the **Task View** icon on the taskbar (looks like two
  overlapping rectangles), or
* Press **Windows key + Tab**.

Task View shows all open windows and a row of desktops at the bottom.

## Creating a new desktop

In Task View, click **New desktop** at the bottom-left, or press
**Windows key + Ctrl + D**.

## Switching between desktops

* Press **Windows key + Ctrl + Left/Right arrow** to flip between
  desktops.
* Or open Task View and click the desktop you want.

## Moving a window to another desktop

In Task View, drag the window's preview onto the desktop tile at the
bottom. You can also right-click a window preview and pick **Move to**.

## Renaming a desktop

In Task View, click the desktop's name at the bottom and type a new
name like "Work" or "Calls".

## Closing a desktop

In Task View, hover over the desktop tile and click the **X**. The
windows on that desktop move to the next desktop — they are not
closed.

## A simpler alternative: minimizing windows

If virtual desktops feel confusing, minimizing windows (clicking the
**−** button in the top-right of any window) keeps them out of the way
without learning Task View.

# Environment variables on Windows 11

Environment variables are pieces of named text the operating system
makes available to every program — for example `%TEMP%` (the user's
temporary folder) or `%PATH%` (where Windows looks for command-line
programs).

## Opening the Environment Variables editor

1. Press **Windows key + R**, type `sysdm.cpl`, press **Enter**.
2. Click the **Advanced** tab.
3. Click **Environment Variables…** at the bottom.

There are two lists:

* **User variables** — apply only to the signed-in user.
* **System variables** — apply to all users on this computer.

## Adding a folder to PATH

`PATH` is a semicolon-separated list of folders. Programs in any of
those folders can be run by name from the command line.

1. In the editor, select **Path** under **User variables**.
2. Click **Edit**.
3. Click **New** and type the folder path, for example
   `C:\Tools\bin`.
4. Click **OK** to close all three dialogs.
5. Open a new terminal window — old terminals still see the old PATH.

## Setting a variable from PowerShell

```
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("MY_VAR", "value", "User")
```

The third argument is `User` or `Machine`. Open a new terminal to see
the new value.

## Common built-in variables

* `%USERPROFILE%` — your home folder, like `C:\Users\Jane`.
* `%APPDATA%` — `C:\Users\Jane\AppData\Roaming`.
* `%LOCALAPPDATA%` — `C:\Users\Jane\AppData\Local`.
* `%TEMP%` — your temporary files folder.
* `%PROGRAMFILES%` — `C:\Program Files`.

## Reverting a bad change

If you accidentally erased PATH and important programs stopped
working, sign out and back in — Windows applies fresh defaults from
the registry. If a system PATH was wiped, restore from a System
Restore point made before your change.

# Virtual desktops and Task View on Windows 11

Virtual desktops let you have several "screens" of open apps without
needing more monitors — for example a desktop for personal browsing
and another for video calls.

## Opening Task View

* Click the **Task View** icon on the taskbar (looks like two
  overlapping rectangles), or
* Press **Windows key + Tab**.

Task View shows all open windows and a row of desktops at the bottom.

## Creating a new desktop

In Task View, click **New desktop** at the bottom-left, or press
**Windows key + Ctrl + D**.

## Switching between desktops

* Press **Windows key + Ctrl + Left/Right arrow** to flip between
  desktops.
* Or open Task View and click the desktop you want.

## Moving a window to another desktop

In Task View, drag the window's preview onto the desktop tile at the
bottom. You can also right-click a window preview and pick **Move to**.

## Renaming a desktop

In Task View, click the desktop's name at the bottom and type a new
name like "Work" or "Calls".

windows on that desktop move to the next desktop — they are not
closed.

## A simpler alternative: minimizing windows

**−** button in the top-right of any window) keeps them out of the way
without learning Task View.

# System Settings overview on macOS

System Settings is where most Mac options live. (On older macOS it
was called **System Preferences**.)

## How to open System Settings

* Click the **Apple menu** (Apple icon) at the top-left of the screen
  and choose **System Settings**, or
* Click the **gear** icon in the Dock if it is there, or
* Press **Command + Space** to open Spotlight, type
  **System Settings**, and press **Return**.

## Where things live

System Settings has a sidebar on the left with these sections:

* **Wi-Fi** — wireless networks.
* **Bluetooth** — wireless device pairing.
* **Network** — Ethernet, VPN, Firewall.
* **General** — About, Software Update, Storage, Sharing.
* **Appearance** — light/dark mode and accent color.
* **Accessibility** — vision, hearing, and motor accommodations.
* **Sound** — volume, output, and input devices.
* **Displays** — resolution, brightness, Night Shift.
* **Privacy & Security** — app permissions, FileVault, Touch ID.
* **Apple ID** — iCloud, App Store, Find My.

## Searching System Settings

There is a search box at the top of the sidebar. Type what you are
looking for — for example "scroll direction" or "default browser".

## When System Settings will not open

If clicking the menu does nothing, force-quit System Settings:

1. Press **Option + Command + Esc**.
2. Pick **System Settings** in the list.
3. Click **Force Quit**.

Then reopen it from the Apple menu.

# Virtual desktops and Task View on Windows 11

Virtual desktops let you have several "screens" of open apps without
needing more monitors — for example a desktop for personal browsing
and another for video calls.

## Opening Task View

* Click the **Task View** icon on the taskbar (looks like two
  overlapping rectangles), or
* Press **Windows key + Tab**.

Task View shows all open windows and a row of desktops at the bottom.

## Creating a new desktop

In Task View, click **New desktop** at the bottom-left, or press
**Windows key + Ctrl + D**.

## Switching between desktops

* Press **Windows key + Ctrl + Left/Right arrow** to flip between
  desktops.
* Or open Task View and click the desktop you want.

## Moving a window to another desktop

In Task View, drag the window's preview onto the desktop tile at the
bottom. You can also right-click a window preview and pick **Move to**.

## Renaming a desktop

In Task View, click the desktop's name at the bottom and type a new
name like "Work" or "Calls".

## Closing a desktop

In Task View, hover over the desktop tile and click the **X**. The
windows on that desktop move to the next desktop — they are not
closed.

## A simpler alternative: minimizing windows

If virtual desktops feel confusing, minimizing windows (clicking the
**−** button in the top-right of any window) keeps them out of the way
without learning Task View.

# Connect to Wi-Fi on Mac

## Connecting to a new network

1. Click the **Wi-Fi icon** in the menu bar at the top-right of the
   screen. The icon looks like a small fan of curved lines.
2. If Wi-Fi is off, click the toggle to turn it on.
3. Choose the Wi-Fi network from the list.
4. Type the password and click **Join**.

The Mac remembers the network and joins automatically when in range.

## Forgetting a network

1. Open **System Settings → Wi-Fi**.
2. Find the network under **Known Networks**.
3. Click the **three dots** next to its name and choose **Forget This
   Network**.

## When Wi-Fi will not connect

Try these in order:

* Click the Wi-Fi icon, toggle Wi-Fi off and back on.
* Open **System Settings → Wi-Fi**, click **Details** next to the
  network, and re-enter the password.
* Restart the Mac.
* Restart the home router (unplug for 30 seconds, plug back in).
* Open **Wireless Diagnostics** by holding **Option** and clicking
  the Wi-Fi icon, then choose **Open Wireless Diagnostics…**.

## Connecting to a hidden network

If the Wi-Fi network does not broadcast its name:

1. Click the Wi-Fi icon.
2. Click **Other Networks**.
3. Click **Other…** at the bottom.
4. Type the network name (SSID) and password.

## Internet works but websites do not load

This usually means a DNS issue. In **System Settings → Wi-Fi**, click
**Details** next to the network, click **DNS**, and add `1.1.1.1` and
`8.8.8.8` as servers.

# System Settings overview on macOS

System Settings is where most Mac options live. (On older macOS it
was called **System Preferences**.)

## How to open System Settings

* Click the **Apple menu** (Apple icon) at the top-left of the screen
  and choose **System Settings**, or
* Click the **gear** icon in the Dock if it is there, or
* Press **Command + Space** to open Spotlight, type
  **System Settings**, and press **Return**.

## Where things live

System Settings has a sidebar on the left with these sections:

* **Wi-Fi** — wireless networks.
* **Bluetooth** — wireless device pairing.
* **Network** — Ethernet, VPN, Firewall.
* **General** — About, Software Update, Storage, Sharing.
* **Appearance** — light/dark mode and accent color.
* **Accessibility** — vision, hearing, and motor accommodations.
* **Sound** — volume, output, and input devices.
* **Displays** — resolution, brightness, Night Shift.
* **Privacy & Security** — app permissions, FileVault, Touch ID.
* **Apple ID** — iCloud, App Store, Find My.

## Searching System Settings

There is a search box at the top of the sidebar. Type what you are
looking for — for example "scroll direction" or "default browser".

## When System Settings will not open

If clicking the menu does nothing, force-quit System Settings:

1. Press **Option + Command + Esc**.
2. Pick **System Settings** in the list.
3. Click **Force Quit**.

Then reopen it from the Apple menu.

# System Settings overview on macOS

System Settings is where most Mac options live. (On older macOS it
was called **System Preferences**.)

## How to open System Settings

* Click the **Apple menu** (Apple icon) at the top-left of the screen
  and choose **System Settings**, or
* Click the **gear** icon in the Dock if it is there, or
* Press **Command + Space** to open Spotlight, type
  **System Settings**, and press **Return**.

## Where things live

System Settings has a sidebar on the left with these sections:

* **Wi-Fi** — wireless networks.
* **Bluetooth** — wireless device pairing.
* **Network** — Ethernet, VPN, Firewall.
* **General** — About, Software Update, Storage, Sharing.
* **Appearance** — light/dark mode and accent color.
* **Accessibility** — vision, hearing, and motor accommodations.
* **Sound** — volume, output, and input devices.
* **Displays** — resolution, brightness, Night Shift.
* **Privacy & Security** — app permissions, FileVault, Touch ID.
* **Apple ID** — iCloud, App Store, Find My.

## Searching System Settings

There is a search box at the top of the sidebar. Type what you are
looking for — for example "scroll direction" or "default browser".

## When System Settings will not open

If clicking the menu does nothing, force-quit System Settings:

1. Press **Option + Command + Esc**.
2. Pick **System Settings** in the list.
3. Click **Force Quit**.

Then reopen it from the Apple menu.

# Connect to Wi-Fi on Mac

## Connecting to a new network

1. Click the **Wi-Fi icon** in the menu bar at the top-right of the
   screen. The icon looks like a small fan of curved lines.
2. If Wi-Fi is off, click the toggle to turn it on.
3. Choose the Wi-Fi network from the list.
4. Type the password and click **Join**.

The Mac remembers the network and joins automatically when in range.

## Forgetting a network

1. Open **System Settings → Wi-Fi**.
2. Find the network under **Known Networks**.
3. Click the **three dots** next to its name and choose **Forget This
   Network**.

## When Wi-Fi will not connect

Try these in order:

* Click the Wi-Fi icon, toggle Wi-Fi off and back on.
* Open **System Settings → Wi-Fi**, click **Details** next to the
  network, and re-enter the password.
* Restart the Mac.
* Restart the home router (unplug for 30 seconds, plug back in).
* Open **Wireless Diagnostics** by holding **Option** and clicking
  the Wi-Fi icon, then choose **Open Wireless Diagnostics…**.

## Connecting to a hidden network

If the Wi-Fi network does not broadcast its name:

1. Click the Wi-Fi icon.
2. Click **Other Networks**.
3. Click **Other…** at the bottom.
4. Type the network name (SSID) and password.

## Internet works but websites do not load

This usually means a DNS issue. In **System Settings → Wi-Fi**, click
**Details** next to the network, click **DNS**, and add `1.1.1.1` and
`8.8.8.8` as servers.

# Pair a Bluetooth device on Mac

## Turning Bluetooth on

* Click the **Control Center** icon (two pills) in the menu bar, then
  click the **Bluetooth** tile, or
* Open **System Settings → Bluetooth** and turn the switch on.

## Pairing a new device

1. Put the device into pairing mode. Most headphones have a button
   you hold for 3-5 seconds until a light flashes.
2. Open **System Settings → Bluetooth**.
3. Wait for the device to appear under **Nearby Devices**.
4. Click **Connect** next to it.
5. If a passcode shows, confirm it on the device.

## Reconnecting a known device

Once paired, the Mac reconnects automatically when the device is on
and in range. Some devices (especially headphones) need to be
manually selected from the Bluetooth menu when first turned on.

## Removing a paired device

1. **System Settings → Bluetooth**.
2. Hover over the device under **My Devices**.
3. Click the **i** (info) icon and choose **Forget This Device**.

## When pairing fails

* Charge the device.
* Move it within 3 feet of the Mac.
* If the device was previously paired with another Mac, iPad, or
  iPhone, unpair it on that other device first.
* Reset the Mac's Bluetooth module: hold **Option + Shift** while
  clicking the Bluetooth icon (older macOS) or use Terminal to run
  `sudo pkill bluetoothd` (admin password required).

## AirPods special behavior

AirPods that have already been linked to your iCloud account pair
automatically when opened near the Mac. Click the volume icon in the
menu bar to choose them as audio output.

# Connect to Wi-Fi on Mac

## Connecting to a new network

1. Click the **Wi-Fi icon** in the menu bar at the top-right of the
   screen. The icon looks like a small fan of curved lines.
2. If Wi-Fi is off, click the toggle to turn it on.
3. Choose the Wi-Fi network from the list.
4. Type the password and click **Join**.

The Mac remembers the network and joins automatically when in range.

## Forgetting a network

1. Open **System Settings → Wi-Fi**.
2. Find the network under **Known Networks**.
3. Click the **three dots** next to its name and choose **Forget This
   Network**.

## When Wi-Fi will not connect

Try these in order:

* Click the Wi-Fi icon, toggle Wi-Fi off and back on.
* Open **System Settings → Wi-Fi**, click **Details** next to the
  network, and re-enter the password.
* Restart the Mac.
* Restart the home router (unplug for 30 seconds, plug back in).
* Open **Wireless Diagnostics** by holding **Option** and clicking
  the Wi-Fi icon, then choose **Open Wireless Diagnostics…**.

## Connecting to a hidden network

If the Wi-Fi network does not broadcast its name:

1. Click the Wi-Fi icon.
2. Click **Other Networks**.
3. Click **Other…** at the bottom.
4. Type the network name (SSID) and password.

## Internet works but websites do not load

This usually means a DNS issue. In **System Settings → Wi-Fi**, click
**Details** next to the network, click **DNS**, and add `1.1.1.1` and
`8.8.8.8` as servers.

# Make text and icons bigger on Mac

## Making the whole screen show bigger items

1. Open **System Settings → Displays**.
2. Under **Resolution**, choose **Larger Text** (older macOS calls
   this **Default for display**).

This makes everything on screen — text, icons, buttons — physically
larger.

## Making just text bigger in apps

* **Mail** — choose **Mail → Settings → Fonts & Colors** and pick a
  larger message font.
* **Messages** — Messages → Settings → General → Text size slider.
* **Safari** — press **Command + plus (+)** to zoom in, **Command +
  0** to reset.
* **Notes** — Notes → Settings → Default text size.

## Make the cursor easier to see

In **System Settings → Accessibility → Display**:

* Toggle **Pointer size** larger.
* Turn on **Shake mouse pointer to locate** — wiggling the mouse
  briefly enlarges the pointer.

## Use Zoom to magnify part of the screen

Zoom enlarges a portion of the screen on demand.

1. **System Settings → Accessibility → Zoom**.
2. Turn on **Use keyboard shortcuts to zoom**:
   * **Option + Command + 8** — toggle Zoom.
   * **Option + Command + plus (=)** — zoom in.
   * **Option + Command + minus (-)** — zoom out.

Or turn on **Use scroll gesture with modifier keys** so you can hold
**Control** and scroll to zoom.

## Make the menu bar text bigger

The menu bar font cannot be changed directly, but increasing display
scaling (above) makes the menu bar bigger along with everything else.

title: Pair a Bluetooth device on Mac

# Pair a Bluetooth device on Mac

## Turning Bluetooth on

* Click the **Control Center** icon (two pills) in the menu bar, then
  click the **Bluetooth** tile, or
* Open **System Settings → Bluetooth** and turn the switch on.

## Pairing a new device

1. Put the device into pairing mode. Most headphones have a button
   you hold for 3-5 seconds until a light flashes.
2. Open **System Settings → Bluetooth**.
3. Wait for the device to appear under **Nearby Devices**.
4. Click **Connect** next to it.
5. If a passcode shows, confirm it on the device.

## Reconnecting a known device

Once paired, the Mac reconnects automatically when the device is on
and in range. Some devices (especially headphones) need to be
manually selected from the Bluetooth menu when first turned on.

## Removing a paired device

1. **System Settings → Bluetooth**.
2. Hover over the device under **My Devices**.
3. Click the **i** (info) icon and choose **Forget This Device**.

## When pairing fails

* Charge the device.
* Move it within 3 feet of the Mac.
* If the device was previously paired with another Mac, iPad, or
  iPhone, unpair it on that other device first.
* Reset the Mac's Bluetooth module: hold **Option + Shift** while
  clicking the Bluetooth icon (older macOS) or use Terminal to run
  `sudo pkill bluetoothd` (admin password required).

## AirPods special behavior

AirPods that have already been linked to your iCloud account pair
automatically when opened near the Mac. Click the volume icon in the
menu bar to choose them as audio output.

# Sound and audio output on Mac

## Adjusting volume

* Use the **F11** and **F12** keys (volume down / volume up). On some
  Macs you must hold **Fn**.
* Or click the **volume icon** in the menu bar and drag the slider.

If the volume icon is missing, open **System Settings → Control
Center**, find **Sound**, and pick **Show in Menu Bar**.

## Choosing audio output

1. Click the **volume icon** in the menu bar.

# Make text and icons bigger on Mac

## Making the whole screen show bigger items

1. Open **System Settings → Displays**.
2. Under **Resolution**, choose **Larger Text** (older macOS calls
   this **Default for display**).

This makes everything on screen — text, icons, buttons — physically
larger.

## Making just text bigger in apps

* **Mail** — choose **Mail → Settings → Fonts & Colors** and pick a
  larger message font.
* **Messages** — Messages → Settings → General → Text size slider.
* **Safari** — press **Command + plus (+)** to zoom in, **Command +
  0** to reset.
* **Notes** — Notes → Settings → Default text size.

## Make the cursor easier to see

In **System Settings → Accessibility → Display**:

* Toggle **Pointer size** larger.
* Turn on **Shake mouse pointer to locate** — wiggling the mouse
  briefly enlarges the pointer.

## Use Zoom to magnify part of the screen

Zoom enlarges a portion of the screen on demand.

1. **System Settings → Accessibility → Zoom**.
2. Turn on **Use keyboard shortcuts to zoom**:
   * **Option + Command + 8** — toggle Zoom.
   * **Option + Command + plus (=)** — zoom in.
   * **Option + Command + minus (-)** — zoom out.

Or turn on **Use scroll gesture with modifier keys** so you can hold
**Control** and scroll to zoom.

## Make the menu bar text bigger

The menu bar font cannot be changed directly, but increasing display
scaling (above) makes the menu bar bigger along with everything else.

# Add a printer on Mac

## USB printer

1. Plug the printer into the Mac with a USB cable.
2. Turn the printer on.
3. macOS usually adds it automatically. The first time you print, it
   will appear in the print dialog's **Printer** dropdown.

If macOS asks to download printer software, allow it.

## Wi-Fi printer

1. Make sure the printer is on the same Wi-Fi network as the Mac.
2. Open **System Settings → Printers & Scanners**.
3. Click **Add Printer, Scanner, or Fax…**.
4. Wait for the printer to appear in the list under the **Default**
   tab.
5. Click the printer and click **Add**.

If the printer does not appear, click the **IP** tab and type the
printer's IP address (you can find it printed on the printer's setup
page or in the router's device list).

## AirPrint vs traditional driver

Most modern printers support **AirPrint** — they work with the Mac
without installing any extra software. The driver dropdown shows
**AirPrint** automatically. If your printer is not AirPrint-capable,
the Mac downloads a driver from Apple. Avoid downloading drivers
from third-party sites.

## Setting a default printer

In **System Settings → Printers & Scanners**, set the **Default
printer** dropdown to the printer you want.

## Clearing a stuck print job

1. **System Settings → Printers & Scanners**.
2. Click the printer.
3. Click **Printer Queue…**.
4. Select the stuck job and click the **X** in its row.

## Printer is offline

* Power-cycle the printer (off, wait 10 seconds, on).
* Make sure the Mac and the printer are on the same Wi-Fi network.
* Remove and re-add the printer in **Printers & Scanners**.

---
title: Sound and audio output on Mac
source_url: https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/change-the-sound-settings-mchlp2230/mac
os: macos
last_verified: 2026-05-07
---

# Sound and audio output on Mac

## Adjusting volume

* Use the **F11** and **F12** keys (volume down / volume up). On some
  Macs you must hold **Fn**.
* Or click the **volume icon** in the menu bar and drag the slider.

If the volume icon is missing, open **System Settings → Control
Center**, find **Sound**, and pick **Show in Menu Bar**.

## Choosing audio output

1. Click the **volume icon** in the menu bar.
2. Under **Output**, click the device you want — Mac speakers,
   headphones, AirPods, or external speakers.

Or open **System Settings → Sound → Output** for the full list.

## When there is no sound

* Make sure the volume is not at zero and not muted.
* In **System Settings → Sound → Output**, verify the right device is
  selected.
* Plug headphones in and out — sometimes the system gets stuck on the
  wrong output.
* Restart the Mac.

If sound still does not work, reset the audio system:

1. Open **Activity Monitor** from **Applications → Utilities**.
2. Search for **coreaudiod**.
3. Click it and press the **X** button to quit it. macOS will restart
   it automatically.

## Microphone not working in calls

* **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone**: make sure
  the app has permission.
* **System Settings → Sound → Input**: pick the correct microphone
  and speak — the level meter should bounce.

## AirPods quieter on calls than music

This is normal. AirPods use a lower-quality audio mode for two-way
calls so the microphone works. Quality returns to normal when the
call ends.

   headphones, AirPods, or external speakers.

* Make sure the volume is not at zero and not muted.

  selected.

# Add a printer on Mac

## USB printer

1. Plug the printer into the Mac with a USB cable.
2. Turn the printer on.
3. macOS usually adds it automatically. The first time you print, it
   will appear in the print dialog's **Printer** dropdown.

If macOS asks to download printer software, allow it.

## Wi-Fi printer

1. Make sure the printer is on the same Wi-Fi network as the Mac.
2. Open **System Settings → Printers & Scanners**.
3. Click **Add Printer, Scanner, or Fax…**.
4. Wait for the printer to appear in the list under the **Default**
   tab.
5. Click the printer and click **Add**.

If the printer does not appear, click the **IP** tab and type the
printer's IP address (you can find it printed on the printer's setup
page or in the router's device list).

## AirPrint vs traditional driver

Most modern printers support **AirPrint** — they work with the Mac
without installing any extra software. The driver dropdown shows
**AirPrint** automatically. If your printer is not AirPrint-capable,
the Mac downloads a driver from Apple. Avoid downloading drivers
from third-party sites.

## Setting a default printer

In **System Settings → Printers & Scanners**, set the **Default
printer** dropdown to the printer you want.

## Clearing a stuck print job

1. **System Settings → Printers & Scanners**.
2. Click the printer.
3. Click **Printer Queue…**.
4. Select the stuck job and click the **X** in its row.

## Printer is offline

* Power-cycle the printer (off, wait 10 seconds, on).
* Make sure the Mac and the printer are on the same Wi-Fi network.
* Remove and re-add the printer in **Printers & Scanners**.

# Software Update on Mac

Software Update keeps macOS, Apple's apps, and security patches
current. Most updates download in the background.

## Check for updates manually

1. Open **System Settings → General → Software Update**.
2. Wait while macOS checks Apple's servers.
3. If updates are available, click **Update Now** or **Upgrade Now**.

## The difference between Update and Upgrade

* **Update** — minor patches within the same macOS version, like
  going from 15.2 to 15.3.
* **Upgrade** — major version change, like going from macOS Sonoma
  to macOS Sequoia.

Upgrades take longer (30-60 minutes) and may require more disk space.
Back up before upgrading.

## Automatic updates

In the same screen, click the **i** next to **Automatic updates** to
configure:

* **Check for updates** — recommend on.
* **Download new updates when available** — recommend on.
* **Install macOS updates** — your choice. Off means you control the
  timing of restarts.
* **Install application updates from the App Store** — recommend on.
* **Install Security Responses and system files** — strongly
  recommend on.

## Update is stuck or failing

* Free up disk space — major upgrades need 30-50 GB free.
* Restart the Mac and try again.
* Connect to a wired Ethernet network instead of Wi-Fi if downloads
  are slow.
* If a partial download is corrupt, run **About This Mac → Storage →
  Manage → Recommendations → Free up storage** to clear caches.

## Beta and developer software

If you accidentally enrolled in the beta program, in
**Software Update**, click the **i** next to **Beta updates** and
choose **Off**.

# Software Update on Mac

Software Update keeps macOS, Apple's apps, and security patches
current. Most updates download in the background.

## Check for updates manually

1. Open **System Settings → General → Software Update**.
2. Wait while macOS checks Apple's servers.
3. If updates are available, click **Update Now** or **Upgrade Now**.

## The difference between Update and Upgrade

* **Update** — minor patches within the same macOS version, like
  going from 15.2 to 15.3.

title: Add a printer on Mac

# Add a printer on Mac

## USB printer

1. Plug the printer into the Mac with a USB cable.
2. Turn the printer on.
3. macOS usually adds it automatically. The first time you print, it
   will appear in the print dialog's **Printer** dropdown.

If macOS asks to download printer software, allow it.

## Wi-Fi printer

1. Make sure the printer is on the same Wi-Fi network as the Mac.
2. Open **System Settings → Printers & Scanners**.
3. Click **Add Printer, Scanner, or Fax…**.
4. Wait for the printer to appear in the list under the **Default**
   tab.
5. Click the printer and click **Add**.

If the printer does not appear, click the **IP** tab and type the
printer's IP address (you can find it printed on the printer's setup
page or in the router's device list).

## AirPrint vs traditional driver

Most modern printers support **AirPrint** — they work with the Mac
without installing any extra software. The driver dropdown shows
**AirPrint** automatically. If your printer is not AirPrint-capable,
the Mac downloads a driver from Apple. Avoid downloading drivers
from third-party sites.

## Setting a default printer

In **System Settings → Printers & Scanners**, set the **Default
printer** dropdown to the printer you want.

## Clearing a stuck print job

1. **System Settings → Printers & Scanners**.
2. Click the printer.
3. Click **Printer Queue…**.
4. Select the stuck job and click the **X** in its row.

## Printer is offline

* Power-cycle the printer (off, wait 10 seconds, on).
* Make sure the Mac and the printer are on the same Wi-Fi network.
* Remove and re-add the printer in **Printers & Scanners**.

# Finder basics on Mac

Finder is the macOS equivalent of File Explorer. It is the program
running whenever you see a desktop or folder window. Its icon is the
**blue and white face** at the left end of the Dock.

## Opening a Finder window

* Click the **Finder** icon in the Dock, or
* Press **Command + N** when Finder is the active app.

## The sidebar

The left side of the window shows your favorite places. By default:

* **AirDrop** — share files with nearby Apple devices.
* **Recents** — files opened recently.
* **Applications** — installed apps.
* **Desktop**, **Documents**, **Downloads** — your personal folders.
* **iCloud Drive** — files synced to iCloud.

You can drag any folder into the sidebar to make it always visible.

## View styles

Look for the four small icons at the top of the Finder window:

* **Icon view** — large pictures.
* **List view** — sortable columns.
* **Column view** — folders cascade left to right.
* **Gallery view** — preview the highlighted file.

## Creating a new folder

* Press **Shift + Command + N**, or
* Right-click empty space and choose **New Folder**.

## Renaming a file or folder

Click the name once (after it is selected), or select it and press
**Return**.

## Searching

The search box at the top right of Finder searches your whole Mac. To
limit the search to the current folder, after pressing search, click
the folder name shown right under the search bar.

## Deleting a file

Drag the file to the **Trash** in the Dock, or select it and press
**Command + Delete**.

# Software Update on Mac

Software Update keeps macOS, Apple's apps, and security patches
current. Most updates download in the background.

## Check for updates manually

1. Open **System Settings → General → Software Update**.
2. Wait while macOS checks Apple's servers.
3. If updates are available, click **Update Now** or **Upgrade Now**.

## The difference between Update and Upgrade

* **Update** — minor patches within the same macOS version, like
  going from 15.2 to 15.3.
* **Upgrade** — major version change, like going from macOS Sonoma
  to macOS Sequoia.

Upgrades take longer (30-60 minutes) and may require more disk space.
Back up before upgrading.

## Automatic updates

In the same screen, click the **i** next to **Automatic updates** to
configure:

* **Check for updates** — recommend on.
* **Download new updates when available** — recommend on.
* **Install macOS updates** — your choice. Off means you control the
  timing of restarts.
* **Install application updates from the App Store** — recommend on.
* **Install Security Responses and system files** — strongly
  recommend on.

## Update is stuck or failing

* Free up disk space — major upgrades need 30-50 GB free.
* Restart the Mac and try again.
* Connect to a wired Ethernet network instead of Wi-Fi if downloads
  are slow.
* If a partial download is corrupt, run **About This Mac → Storage →
  Manage → Recommendations → Free up storage** to clear caches.

## Beta and developer software

If you accidentally enrolled in the beta program, in
**Software Update**, click the **i** next to **Beta updates** and
choose **Off**.

# The Dock and menu bar on Mac

The **Dock** is the row of icons at the bottom of the screen. The
**menu bar** is the strip at the top.

## Adding an app to the Dock

* Drag the app's icon from **Applications** onto the Dock, or
* Right-click a running app's Dock icon and choose **Options → Keep
  in Dock**.

## Removing an app from the Dock

Drag the icon away from the Dock until you see **Remove** appear, then
release. (The app itself is not deleted — only the Dock shortcut.)

## Moving the Dock to the side

The Dock can sit at the bottom, left, or right.

1. Open **System Settings → Desktop & Dock**.
2. Find **Position on screen** and choose **Left**, **Bottom**, or
   **Right**.

## Hiding the Dock

In the same panel, turn on **Automatically hide and show the Dock**.
The Dock disappears until you move the mouse to its edge of the
screen.

## Magnification

Turn on **Magnification** for icons to grow as you point at them — a
nice readability help.

## The menu bar

Apple icon, app menus, status icons (Wi-Fi, battery, Control Center,
clock) — all live in the menu bar at the top of the screen.

## Adding or removing menu bar icons

1. **System Settings → Control Center**.
2. For each item, choose **Show in Menu Bar**, **Don't Show in Menu
   Bar**, or only in Control Center.

## Dragging menu bar icons

Hold **Command** and drag any menu bar icon left or right to reorder
it. You can drag third-party icons off the menu bar entirely (some
apps will re-add them next launch).

# Finder basics on Mac

Finder is the macOS equivalent of File Explorer. It is the program
running whenever you see a desktop or folder window. Its icon is the
**blue and white face** at the left end of the Dock.

## Opening a Finder window

* Click the **Finder** icon in the Dock, or
* Press **Command + N** when Finder is the active app.

## The sidebar

The left side of the window shows your favorite places. By default:

* **AirDrop** — share files with nearby Apple devices.
* **Recents** — files opened recently.
* **Applications** — installed apps.
* **Desktop**, **Documents**, **Downloads** — your personal folders.
* **iCloud Drive** — files synced to iCloud.

You can drag any folder into the sidebar to make it always visible.

## View styles

Look for the four small icons at the top of the Finder window:

* **Icon view** — large pictures.
* **List view** — sortable columns.
* **Column view** — folders cascade left to right.
* **Gallery view** — preview the highlighted file.

* Press **Shift + Command + N**, or
* Right-click empty space and choose **New Folder**.

**Return**.

The search box at the top right of Finder searches your whole Mac. To
limit the search to the current folder, after pressing search, click
the folder name shown right under the search bar.

## Deleting a file

Drag the file to the **Trash** in the Dock, or select it and press
**Command + Delete**.

# Spotlight search on Mac

Spotlight is the Mac's universal search. Use it to find files, open
apps, do quick math, and look up definitions.

## Opening Spotlight

Press **Command + Space**. A search box appears at the top of the
screen.

## What you can search for

* **App names** — type **Mail**, **Safari**, **Calculator**, etc.,
  then press **Return** to launch.
* **Documents** — type the file name or words from inside the file.
* **Settings** — type **Wi-Fi**, **Sound**, **Bluetooth**, etc.
* **Math** — type `(125 * 3) + 7`, the answer appears.
* **Conversions** — `100 USD in EUR`, `5 miles to km`.
* **Definitions** — type a word and look for the dictionary preview.
* **Web search** — at the bottom of results, **Search Web for…**.

## Refining results

Spotlight previews each result on the right. Use the up/down arrows
to scroll.

To open the highlighted item:
* Press **Return** to open it.
* Press **Command + Return** to show it in Finder instead of opening.

## Hiding categories you do not use

1. **System Settings → Spotlight**.
2. Uncheck categories like **Movies**, **Sports**, **Stocks** if you
   never search those.

## Excluding a folder from search

In the same Spotlight panel, click the **Search Privacy** button at
the bottom. Drag any folder you want excluded into the list. Useful
for keeping confidential files out of search results.

# The Dock and menu bar on Mac

The **Dock** is the row of icons at the bottom of the screen. The
**menu bar** is the strip at the top.

## Adding an app to the Dock

* Drag the app's icon from **Applications** onto the Dock, or
* Right-click a running app's Dock icon and choose **Options → Keep
  in Dock**.

## Removing an app from the Dock

Drag the icon away from the Dock until you see **Remove** appear, then
release. (The app itself is not deleted — only the Dock shortcut.)

## Moving the Dock to the side

The Dock can sit at the bottom, left, or right.

1. Open **System Settings → Desktop & Dock**.
2. Find **Position on screen** and choose **Left**, **Bottom**, or
   **Right**.

## Hiding the Dock

In the same panel, turn on **Automatically hide and show the Dock**.
The Dock disappears until you move the mouse to its edge of the
screen.

## Magnification

Turn on **Magnification** for icons to grow as you point at them — a
nice readability help.

## The menu bar

Apple icon, app menus, status icons (Wi-Fi, battery, Control Center,
clock) — all live in the menu bar at the top of the screen.

## Adding or removing menu bar icons

1. **System Settings → Control Center**.
2. For each item, choose **Show in Menu Bar**, **Don't Show in Menu
   Bar**, or only in Control Center.

## Dragging menu bar icons

Hold **Command** and drag any menu bar icon left or right to reorder
it. You can drag third-party icons off the menu bar entirely (some
apps will re-add them next launch).

# Accessibility and VoiceOver on Mac

macOS has a single hub for accessibility under **System Settings →
Accessibility**.

## Vision

* **Display** — make text bigger, increase contrast, reduce motion,
  invert colors.
* **Zoom** — magnify part of the screen with a keyboard shortcut.
* **VoiceOver** — full screen reader that speaks every interface
  element. Toggle with **Command + F5**.
* **Spoken Content** — have the Mac read selected text out loud.

## Hearing

* **Audio** — flash the screen instead of beeping, play stereo as
  mono, balance left/right channels.
* **Captions** — built-in caption preferences for movies and calls.
* **RTT** — Real-time text for phone calls.

## Motor

* **Voice Control** — fully control the Mac by speaking. Turn on in
  Accessibility → Voice Control.
* **Keyboard** — Sticky Keys, Slow Keys, accessibility keyboard.
* **Pointer Control** — alternate ways to control the cursor (head
  pointer, switch control).

## VoiceOver basics

After turning VoiceOver on with **Command + F5**:

* **VO key** — by default this is **Control + Option** (held
  together). Almost every VoiceOver shortcut starts with VO.
* **VO + A** — start reading from the current location.
* **VO + Right Arrow / Left Arrow** — move to the next/previous item.
* **VO + Space** — activate (click) the focused item.

The first time VoiceOver runs, it offers an interactive tutorial.
Take it — VoiceOver is powerful but has a learning curve.

## Quick toggle for accessibility features

Press **Option + Command + F5** to open the **Accessibility
Shortcuts** panel. Check the boxes next to features you want to
toggle quickly from this panel later.

# Spotlight search on Mac

Spotlight is the Mac's universal search. Use it to find files, open
apps, do quick math, and look up definitions.

## Opening Spotlight

Press **Command + Space**. A search box appears at the top of the
screen.

## What you can search for

* **App names** — type **Mail**, **Safari**, **Calculator**, etc.,
  then press **Return** to launch.
* **Documents** — type the file name or words from inside the file.
* **Settings** — type **Wi-Fi**, **Sound**, **Bluetooth**, etc.
* **Math** — type `(125 * 3) + 7`, the answer appears.
* **Conversions** — `100 USD in EUR`, `5 miles to km`.
* **Definitions** — type a word and look for the dictionary preview.
* **Web search** — at the bottom of results, **Search Web for…**.

## Refining results

Spotlight previews each result on the right. Use the up/down arrows
to scroll.

To open the highlighted item:
* Press **Return** to open it.
* Press **Command + Return** to show it in Finder instead of opening.

## Hiding categories you do not use

1. **System Settings → Spotlight**.
2. Uncheck categories like **Movies**, **Sports**, **Stocks** if you
   never search those.

## Excluding a folder from search

In the same Spotlight panel, click the **Search Privacy** button at
the bottom. Drag any folder you want excluded into the list. Useful
for keeping confidential files out of search results.

# Accessibility and VoiceOver on Mac

macOS has a single hub for accessibility under **System Settings →
Accessibility**.

## Vision

* **Display** — make text bigger, increase contrast, reduce motion,
  invert colors.
* **Zoom** — magnify part of the screen with a keyboard shortcut.
* **VoiceOver** — full screen reader that speaks every interface
  element. Toggle with **Command + F5**.
* **Spoken Content** — have the Mac read selected text out loud.

## Hearing

* **Audio** — flash the screen instead of beeping, play stereo as
  mono, balance left/right channels.
* **Captions** — built-in caption preferences for movies and calls.
* **RTT** — Real-time text for phone calls.

## Motor

* **Voice Control** — fully control the Mac by speaking. Turn on in
  Accessibility → Voice Control.
* **Keyboard** — Sticky Keys, Slow Keys, accessibility keyboard.
* **Pointer Control** — alternate ways to control the cursor (head
  pointer, switch control).

## VoiceOver basics

After turning VoiceOver on with **Command + F5**:

* **VO key** — by default this is **Control + Option** (held
  together). Almost every VoiceOver shortcut starts with VO.
* **VO + A** — start reading from the current location.
* **VO + Right Arrow / Left Arrow** — move to the next/previous item.
* **VO + Space** — activate (click) the focused item.

The first time VoiceOver runs, it offers an interactive tutorial.
Take it — VoiceOver is powerful but has a learning curve.

## Quick toggle for accessibility features

Press **Option + Command + F5** to open the **Accessibility
Shortcuts** panel. Check the boxes next to features you want to
toggle quickly from this panel later.

# Apple ID and iCloud on Mac

Your Apple ID is the email address you use for the App Store, iCloud,
iMessage, and FaceTime. iCloud is Apple's cloud storage that syncs
between Mac, iPhone, and iPad.

## Signing in to your Apple ID

1. Open **System Settings**.
2. Click **Sign in** at the top of the sidebar.
3. Enter your Apple ID email and password.
4. Approve the sign-in on another Apple device if prompted.

## What iCloud syncs

In **System Settings → Apple ID → iCloud**, choose what to sync:

* **iCloud Drive** — files in Documents and Desktop folders.
* **Photos** — your photo library.
* **Mail**, **Contacts**, **Calendars**, **Reminders**, **Notes**.
* **Safari** — bookmarks, tabs, passwords.
* **iCloud Keychain** — saved passwords across devices.
* **Find My Mac** — locate the Mac if it is lost.

## Free vs paid iCloud storage

Every Apple ID gets 5 GB of iCloud free. Paid plans:

* **iCloud+ 50 GB** — small monthly fee.
* **iCloud+ 200 GB** — common family plan.
* **iCloud+ 2 TB** — heavy use.

Manage in **System Settings → Apple ID → iCloud → Manage Account
Storage**.

## Two-factor authentication

When you sign in to a new device, Apple sends a 6-digit code to your
trusted devices. Always enable two-factor authentication.

If you lose access to your trusted devices, see Apple's account
recovery process at **iforgot.apple.com**.

## Signing out

In **System Settings → Apple ID**, scroll to the bottom and click
**Sign Out**. macOS asks whether to keep a copy of iCloud files
locally — say yes if you want to keep editing offline.

# Accessibility and VoiceOver on Mac

macOS has a single hub for accessibility under **System Settings →
Accessibility**.

## Vision

* **Display** — make text bigger, increase contrast, reduce motion,
  invert colors.
* **Zoom** — magnify part of the screen with a keyboard shortcut.
* **VoiceOver** — full screen reader that speaks every interface
  element. Toggle with **Command + F5**.
* **Spoken Content** — have the Mac read selected text out loud.

## Hearing

* **Audio** — flash the screen instead of beeping, play stereo as
  mono, balance left/right channels.
* **Captions** — built-in caption preferences for movies and calls.
* **RTT** — Real-time text for phone calls.

## Motor

* **Voice Control** — fully control the Mac by speaking. Turn on in
  Accessibility → Voice Control.
* **Keyboard** — Sticky Keys, Slow Keys, accessibility keyboard.
* **Pointer Control** — alternate ways to control the cursor (head
  pointer, switch control).

## VoiceOver basics

After turning VoiceOver on with **Command + F5**:

* **VO key** — by default this is **Control + Option** (held
  together). Almost every VoiceOver shortcut starts with VO.
* **VO + A** — start reading from the current location.
* **VO + Right Arrow / Left Arrow** — move to the next/previous item.
* **VO + Space** — activate (click) the focused item.

The first time VoiceOver runs, it offers an interactive tutorial.
Take it — VoiceOver is powerful but has a learning curve.

## Quick toggle for accessibility features

Press **Option + Command + F5** to open the **Accessibility
Shortcuts** panel. Check the boxes next to features you want to
toggle quickly from this panel later.

between Mac, iPhone, and iPad.

## Signing in to your Apple ID

1. Open **System Settings**.
2. Click **Sign in** at the top of the sidebar.
3. Enter your Apple ID email and password.
4. Approve the sign-in on another Apple device if prompted.

## What iCloud syncs

In **System Settings → Apple ID → iCloud**, choose what to sync:

* **iCloud Drive** — files in Documents and Desktop folders.
* **Photos** — your photo library.
* **Mail**, **Contacts**, **Calendars**, **Reminders**, **Notes**.
* **Safari** — bookmarks, tabs, passwords.
* **iCloud Keychain** — saved passwords across devices.
* **Find My Mac** — locate the Mac if it is lost.

## Free vs paid iCloud storage

Every Apple ID gets 5 GB of iCloud free. Paid plans:

* **iCloud+ 50 GB** — small monthly fee.
* **iCloud+ 200 GB** — common family plan.
* **iCloud+ 2 TB** — heavy use.

Manage in **System Settings → Apple ID → iCloud → Manage Account
Storage**.

## Two-factor authentication

When you sign in to a new device, Apple sends a 6-digit code to your
trusted devices. Always enable two-factor authentication.

If you lose access to your trusted devices, see Apple's account
recovery process at **iforgot.apple.com**.

## Signing out

In **System Settings → Apple ID**, scroll to the bottom and click
**Sign Out**. macOS asks whether to keep a copy of iCloud files
locally — say yes if you want to keep editing offline.

# Time Machine backup on Mac

Time Machine is Apple's built-in backup. It copies the whole Mac to
an external drive every hour, keeping a history of every change so
you can restore any older version of any file.

## What you need

* An external USB or Thunderbolt hard drive at least 2× the size of
  the Mac's drive (more is better).
* Or a network share — a Time Capsule, AirPort, or many modern NAS
  devices.

## Setting up Time Machine

1. Plug in the external drive.
2. macOS may ask **Do you want to use this drive with Time Machine?**
   — click **Use as Backup Disk**.
3. If it does not ask, open **System Settings → General → Time
   Machine → Add Backup Disk** and pick the drive.
4. Choose whether to encrypt the backup (strongly recommended for
   external drives).

The first backup takes hours — leave the drive plugged in overnight.
Future backups are fast because only changes are copied.

## Restoring a file

1. With the Time Machine drive connected, click the Time Machine
   icon in the menu bar (or open it from Spotlight).
2. Click **Browse Time Machine Backups**.
3. Use the timeline on the right to scroll back to before the file
   was lost.
4. Find the file or folder, click **Restore**.

The file returns to its original location.

## Restoring the whole Mac to a new computer

1. Connect the backup drive to the new Mac.
2. During the new Mac's setup, choose **Migration Assistant → From a
   Mac, Time Machine backup, or Startup disk**.
3. Pick the backup and let it copy your apps, settings, and files.

## Removing old backups to free space

Time Machine deletes the oldest backups automatically when the drive
fills. You usually do not need to do anything — but if you want to
delete a specific snapshot, browse Time Machine, find the date, and
choose **Delete All Backups of [date]** from the gear menu.

# Apple ID and iCloud on Mac

Your Apple ID is the email address you use for the App Store, iCloud,
iMessage, and FaceTime. iCloud is Apple's cloud storage that syncs
between Mac, iPhone, and iPad.

## Signing in to your Apple ID

1. Open **System Settings**.
2. Click **Sign in** at the top of the sidebar.
3. Enter your Apple ID email and password.
4. Approve the sign-in on another Apple device if prompted.

## What iCloud syncs

In **System Settings → Apple ID → iCloud**, choose what to sync:

* **iCloud Drive** — files in Documents and Desktop folders.
* **Photos** — your photo library.
* **Mail**, **Contacts**, **Calendars**, **Reminders**, **Notes**.
* **Safari** — bookmarks, tabs, passwords.
* **iCloud Keychain** — saved passwords across devices.
* **Find My Mac** — locate the Mac if it is lost.

## Free vs paid iCloud storage

Every Apple ID gets 5 GB of iCloud free. Paid plans:

* **iCloud+ 50 GB** — small monthly fee.
* **iCloud+ 200 GB** — common family plan.
* **iCloud+ 2 TB** — heavy use.

Manage in **System Settings → Apple ID → iCloud → Manage Account
Storage**.

## Two-factor authentication

When you sign in to a new device, Apple sends a 6-digit code to your
trusted devices. Always enable two-factor authentication.

If you lose access to your trusted devices, see Apple's account
recovery process at **iforgot.apple.com**.

## Signing out

In **System Settings → Apple ID**, scroll to the bottom and click
**Sign Out**. macOS asks whether to keep a copy of iCloud files
locally — say yes if you want to keep editing offline.

# Time Machine backup on Mac

Time Machine is Apple's built-in backup. It copies the whole Mac to
an external drive every hour, keeping a history of every change so
you can restore any older version of any file.

## What you need

* An external USB or Thunderbolt hard drive at least 2× the size of
  the Mac's drive (more is better).
* Or a network share — a Time Capsule, AirPort, or many modern NAS
  devices.

## Setting up Time Machine

1. Plug in the external drive.
2. macOS may ask **Do you want to use this drive with Time Machine?**
   — click **Use as Backup Disk**.
3. If it does not ask, open **System Settings → General → Time
   Machine → Add Backup Disk** and pick the drive.
4. Choose whether to encrypt the backup (strongly recommended for
   external drives).

The first backup takes hours — leave the drive plugged in overnight.
Future backups are fast because only changes are copied.

## Restoring a file

1. With the Time Machine drive connected, click the Time Machine
   icon in the menu bar (or open it from Spotlight).
2. Click **Browse Time Machine Backups**.
3. Use the timeline on the right to scroll back to before the file
   was lost.
4. Find the file or folder, click **Restore**.

The file returns to its original location.

## Restoring the whole Mac to a new computer

1. Connect the backup drive to the new Mac.
2. During the new Mac's setup, choose **Migration Assistant → From a
   Mac, Time Machine backup, or Startup disk**.
3. Pick the backup and let it copy your apps, settings, and files.

## Removing old backups to free space

Time Machine deletes the oldest backups automatically when the drive
fills. You usually do not need to do anything — but if you want to
delete a specific snapshot, browse Time Machine, find the date, and
choose **Delete All Backups of [date]** from the gear menu.

# Trackpad and mouse on Mac

## Trackpad gestures

* **Tap** — light tap to click (if **Tap to click** is enabled).
* **Two-finger scroll** — scroll up and down.
* **Pinch** — zoom in and out (Photos, Safari, PDF).
* **Two-finger swipe between pages** — back/forward in Safari.
* **Three-finger swipe up** — Mission Control.
* **Three-finger swipe down** — App Exposé (windows of the current app).
* **Three-finger swipe left/right** — switch full-screen apps and
  desktops.
* **Pinch with thumb and three fingers** — Launchpad.
* **Spread thumb and three fingers** — show desktop.

Configure all of these in **System Settings → Trackpad**.

## Pointer speed

Drag the **Tracking speed** slider in **System Settings → Trackpad
→ Point & Click**.

## Right-click on a Mac

* **Two-finger tap** on the trackpad, or
* **Control + click** with one finger, or
* On a Magic Mouse: tap the right side (enable **Secondary click** in
  **System Settings → Mouse**).

## Force click

Pressing the trackpad firmly does extra actions in some apps:

* In Safari: a Force click on a word looks it up in the dictionary.
* In Mail: a Force click on an address creates a Calendar event.

Turn this on or off in **System Settings → Trackpad → Point & Click
→ Force Click and haptic feedback**.

## Natural scrolling

Macs default to **natural scrolling** — the page moves with your
fingers, like a touchscreen. If you prefer the older direction:

1. **System Settings → Trackpad → Scroll & Zoom**.
2. Turn off **Natural scrolling**.

## When the trackpad jumps around

Crumbs or moisture can make the trackpad register false touches.
Wipe the trackpad with a slightly damp microfiber cloth and dry
hands. If the cursor still misbehaves, restart the Mac.

# Trackpad and mouse on Mac

## Trackpad gestures

* **Tap** — light tap to click (if **Tap to click** is enabled).
* **Two-finger scroll** — scroll up and down.
* **Pinch** — zoom in and out (Photos, Safari, PDF).
* **Two-finger swipe between pages** — back/forward in Safari.
* **Three-finger swipe up** — Mission Control.
* **Three-finger swipe down** — App Exposé (windows of the current app).
* **Three-finger swipe left/right** — switch full-screen apps and
  desktops.
* **Pinch with thumb and three fingers** — Launchpad.
* **Spread thumb and three fingers** — show desktop.

Configure all of these in **System Settings → Trackpad**.

## Pointer speed

Drag the **Tracking speed** slider in **System Settings → Trackpad
→ Point & Click**.

## Right-click on a Mac

* **Two-finger tap** on the trackpad, or
* **Control + click** with one finger, or
* On a Magic Mouse: tap the right side (enable **Secondary click** in
  **System Settings → Mouse**).

## Force click

Pressing the trackpad firmly does extra actions in some apps:

* In Safari: a Force click on a word looks it up in the dictionary.
* In Mail: a Force click on an address creates a Calendar event.

Turn this on or off in **System Settings → Trackpad → Point & Click
→ Force Click and haptic feedback**.

## Natural scrolling

Macs default to **natural scrolling** — the page moves with your
fingers, like a touchscreen. If you prefer the older direction:

1. **System Settings → Trackpad → Scroll & Zoom**.
2. Turn off **Natural scrolling**.

## When the trackpad jumps around

Crumbs or moisture can make the trackpad register false touches.
Wipe the trackpad with a slightly damp microfiber cloth and dry
hands. If the cursor still misbehaves, restart the Mac.

# Time Machine backup on Mac

Time Machine is Apple's built-in backup. It copies the whole Mac to
an external drive every hour, keeping a history of every change so
you can restore any older version of any file.

## What you need

* An external USB or Thunderbolt hard drive at least 2× the size of
  the Mac's drive (more is better).
* Or a network share — a Time Capsule, AirPort, or many modern NAS
  devices.

## Setting up Time Machine

1. Plug in the external drive.
2. macOS may ask **Do you want to use this drive with Time Machine?**
   — click **Use as Backup Disk**.
3. If it does not ask, open **System Settings → General → Time
   Machine → Add Backup Disk** and pick the drive.
4. Choose whether to encrypt the backup (strongly recommended for
   external drives).

The first backup takes hours — leave the drive plugged in overnight.
Future backups are fast because only changes are copied.

## Restoring a file

1. With the Time Machine drive connected, click the Time Machine
   icon in the menu bar (or open it from Spotlight).
2. Click **Browse Time Machine Backups**.
3. Use the timeline on the right to scroll back to before the file
   was lost.
4. Find the file or folder, click **Restore**.

The file returns to its original location.

## Restoring the whole Mac to a new computer

1. Connect the backup drive to the new Mac.
2. During the new Mac's setup, choose **Migration Assistant → From a
   Mac, Time Machine backup, or Startup disk**.
3. Pick the backup and let it copy your apps, settings, and files.

## Removing old backups to free space

Time Machine deletes the oldest backups automatically when the drive
fills. You usually do not need to do anything — but if you want to
delete a specific snapshot, browse Time Machine, find the date, and
choose **Delete All Backups of [date]** from the gear menu.

# Trackpad and mouse on Mac

## Trackpad gestures

* **Tap** — light tap to click (if **Tap to click** is enabled).
* **Two-finger scroll** — scroll up and down.
* **Pinch** — zoom in and out (Photos, Safari, PDF).
* **Two-finger swipe between pages** — back/forward in Safari.
* **Three-finger swipe up** — Mission Control.
* **Three-finger swipe down** — App Exposé (windows of the current app).
* **Three-finger swipe left/right** — switch full-screen apps and
  desktops.
* **Pinch with thumb and three fingers** — Launchpad.
* **Spread thumb and three fingers** — show desktop.

Configure all of these in **System Settings → Trackpad**.

## Pointer speed

Drag the **Tracking speed** slider in **System Settings → Trackpad
→ Point & Click**.

## Right-click on a Mac

* **Two-finger tap** on the trackpad, or
* **Control + click** with one finger, or
* On a Magic Mouse: tap the right side (enable **Secondary click** in
  **System Settings → Mouse**).

## Force click

Pressing the trackpad firmly does extra actions in some apps:

* In Safari: a Force click on a word looks it up in the dictionary.
* In Mail: a Force click on an address creates a Calendar event.

Turn this on or off in **System Settings → Trackpad → Point & Click
→ Force Click and haptic feedback**.

## Natural scrolling

Macs default to **natural scrolling** — the page moves with your
fingers, like a touchscreen. If you prefer the older direction:

1. **System Settings → Trackpad → Scroll & Zoom**.
2. Turn off **Natural scrolling**.

## When the trackpad jumps around

Crumbs or moisture can make the trackpad register false touches.
Wipe the trackpad with a slightly damp microfiber cloth and dry
hands. If the cursor still misbehaves, restart the Mac.

# Appearance, dark mode, and Night Shift on Mac

## Switching between light and dark mode

1. Open **System Settings → Appearance**.
2. Pick **Light**, **Dark**, or **Auto** (light during the day, dark
   at night).

Most modern apps respect this choice. Some older apps stay light
regardless.

## Accent color

The accent color is used for buttons, selections, and highlights.

In the same Appearance panel, choose any of the colored circles —
**Multicolor** uses the per-app default.

## Highlight color

Choose the color of selected text in **Appearance → Highlight color**.
Default is the accent color.

## Sidebar icon size

Three options — **Small**, **Medium**, **Large**. Larger sidebar icons
are easier to read.

## Reduce motion (less animation)

If animations cause discomfort:

1. **System Settings → Accessibility → Display**.
2. Turn on **Reduce motion**.

## Night Shift

Night Shift makes the screen warmer (less blue) in the evening, which
can help you wind down.

1. **System Settings → Displays → Night Shift**.
2. Pick **Sunset to Sunrise** for an automatic schedule, or set a
   custom schedule.
3. Drag **Color temperature** toward **More warm** for stronger
   effect.

## True Tone

True Tone subtly adjusts the screen's white balance to match the
room's lighting. Toggle in **Displays**. It is on by default and most
people find it pleasant.

2. Pick **Light**, **Dark**, or **Auto** (light during the day, dark
   at night).

regardless.

## Accent color

The accent color is used for buttons, selections, and highlights.

In the same Appearance panel, choose any of the colored circles —
**Multicolor** uses the per-app default.

## Highlight color

Choose the color of selected text in **Appearance → Highlight color**.
Default is the accent color.

## Sidebar icon size

Three options — **Small**, **Medium**, **Large**. Larger sidebar icons
are easier to read.

If animations cause discomfort:

1. **System Settings → Accessibility → Display**.
2. Turn on **Reduce motion**.

Night Shift makes the screen warmer (less blue) in the evening, which
can help you wind down.

1. **System Settings → Displays → Night Shift**.
2. Pick **Sunset to Sunrise** for an automatic schedule, or set a
   custom schedule.
3. Drag **Color temperature** toward **More warm** for stronger
   effect.

# Trackpad and mouse on Mac

## Trackpad gestures

* **Tap** — light tap to click (if **Tap to click** is enabled).
* **Two-finger scroll** — scroll up and down.
* **Pinch** — zoom in and out (Photos, Safari, PDF).
* **Two-finger swipe between pages** — back/forward in Safari.
* **Three-finger swipe up** — Mission Control.
* **Three-finger swipe down** — App Exposé (windows of the current app).
* **Three-finger swipe left/right** — switch full-screen apps and
  desktops.
* **Pinch with thumb and three fingers** — Launchpad.
* **Spread thumb and three fingers** — show desktop.

Configure all of these in **System Settings → Trackpad**.

## Pointer speed

Drag the **Tracking speed** slider in **System Settings → Trackpad
→ Point & Click**.

## Right-click on a Mac

* **Two-finger tap** on the trackpad, or
* **Control + click** with one finger, or
* On a Magic Mouse: tap the right side (enable **Secondary click** in
  **System Settings → Mouse**).

## Force click

Pressing the trackpad firmly does extra actions in some apps:

* In Safari: a Force click on a word looks it up in the dictionary.
* In Mail: a Force click on an address creates a Calendar event.

Turn this on or off in **System Settings → Trackpad → Point & Click
→ Force Click and haptic feedback**.

## Natural scrolling

Macs default to **natural scrolling** — the page moves with your
fingers, like a touchscreen. If you prefer the older direction:

1. **System Settings → Trackpad → Scroll & Zoom**.
2. Turn off **Natural scrolling**.

## When the trackpad jumps around

Crumbs or moisture can make the trackpad register false touches.
Wipe the trackpad with a slightly damp microfiber cloth and dry
hands. If the cursor still misbehaves, restart the Mac.

# Notifications and Focus on Mac

Notifications appear at the top-right corner of the screen and stack
in **Notification Center**, opened by clicking the date and time in
the menu bar.

## Per-app notification control

1. Open **System Settings → Notifications**.
2. Click an app in the list.
3. Toggle **Allow notifications**.
4. Choose **Banner** (auto-disappear) or **Alert** (stays until
   dismissed).
5. Toggle **Show on Lock Screen** if you want privacy.

## Turn off notification sounds

Per app: **System Settings → Notifications**, click the app, turn off
**Play sound for notifications**.

System-wide: lower the alert volume in **System Settings → Sound →
Sound Effects**.

## Focus modes

Focus is macOS's "do not disturb" with personalities. Modes you can
turn on include:

* **Do Not Disturb** — silence everything.
* **Personal** — allow only personal contacts.
* **Work** — allow work apps and people.
* **Sleep** — silent during scheduled sleep hours.

## Turning Focus on or off

* Click **Control Center** in the menu bar, click **Focus**, pick a
  mode.
* Or set up automatic schedules in **System Settings → Focus**.

## Sharing Focus across devices

In **System Settings → Focus → Share across devices**, turn it on so
turning Focus on at your iPhone also silences your Mac (and vice
versa).

## When notifications are missing

* Make sure **Do Not Disturb** is not on.
* Check the app has notification permission.
* Some apps need their own notification toggles enabled inside the
  app, not just in System Settings.
* Restart the Mac if everything looks correct but no notifications
  arrive.

# Appearance, dark mode, and Night Shift on Mac

## Switching between light and dark mode

1. Open **System Settings → Appearance**.
2. Pick **Light**, **Dark**, or **Auto** (light during the day, dark
   at night).

Most modern apps respect this choice. Some older apps stay light
regardless.

## Accent color

The accent color is used for buttons, selections, and highlights.

In the same Appearance panel, choose any of the colored circles —
**Multicolor** uses the per-app default.

## Highlight color

Choose the color of selected text in **Appearance → Highlight color**.
Default is the accent color.

## Sidebar icon size

Three options — **Small**, **Medium**, **Large**. Larger sidebar icons
are easier to read.

## Reduce motion (less animation)

If animations cause discomfort:

1. **System Settings → Accessibility → Display**.
2. Turn on **Reduce motion**.

## Night Shift

Night Shift makes the screen warmer (less blue) in the evening, which
can help you wind down.

1. **System Settings → Displays → Night Shift**.
2. Pick **Sunset to Sunrise** for an automatic schedule, or set a
   custom schedule.
3. Drag **Color temperature** toward **More warm** for stronger
   effect.

## True Tone

True Tone subtly adjusts the screen's white balance to match the
room's lighting. Toggle in **Displays**. It is on by default and most
people find it pleasant.

# Notifications and Focus on Mac

Notifications appear at the top-right corner of the screen and stack
in **Notification Center**, opened by clicking the date and time in
the menu bar.

## Per-app notification control

1. Open **System Settings → Notifications**.
2. Click an app in the list.
3. Toggle **Allow notifications**.
4. Choose **Banner** (auto-disappear) or **Alert** (stays until
   dismissed).
5. Toggle **Show on Lock Screen** if you want privacy.

## Turn off notification sounds

Per app: **System Settings → Notifications**, click the app, turn off
**Play sound for notifications**.

System-wide: lower the alert volume in **System Settings → Sound →
Sound Effects**.

## Focus modes

Focus is macOS's "do not disturb" with personalities. Modes you can
turn on include:

* **Do Not Disturb** — silence everything.
* **Personal** — allow only personal contacts.
* **Work** — allow work apps and people.
* **Sleep** — silent during scheduled sleep hours.

## Turning Focus on or off

* Click **Control Center** in the menu bar, click **Focus**, pick a
  mode.
* Or set up automatic schedules in **System Settings → Focus**.

## Sharing Focus across devices

In **System Settings → Focus → Share across devices**, turn it on so
turning Focus on at your iPhone also silences your Mac (and vice
versa).

## When notifications are missing

* Make sure **Do Not Disturb** is not on.
* Check the app has notification permission.
* Some apps need their own notification toggles enabled inside the
  app, not just in System Settings.
* Restart the Mac if everything looks correct but no notifications
  arrive.
"},"tool_use_id":"toolu_01QomQa5wC47gQtTf9uy4dBY"}

# Set the default web browser and email app on Mac

When you click a link, macOS opens it in the **default browser**.
When you click a `mailto:` link, macOS opens the **default email
client**.

## Default web browser

1. Open **System Settings → Desktop & Dock**.
2. Scroll to **Default web browser**.
3. Choose Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or any installed browser.

## Default email client

This setting lives inside the Mail app, not System Settings.

1. Open **Mail**.
2. Go to **Mail → Settings → General**.
3. Pick a different app from **Default email reader**.

## What happens when the default browser is uninstalled

If the default browser is no longer installed, macOS falls back to
**Safari**. Set a new default before uninstalling the previous one to
avoid surprises.

## Open links from a specific app in a different browser

Some apps offer their own per-app browser preference. For example,
the Slack desktop app has **Slack → Preferences → Advanced → Open all
links in a default browser**.

## Why a setting keeps reverting

A few apps re-prompt for default-browser status on every launch.
Decline if you do not want them as default — Apple's setting in
**Desktop & Dock** is what actually controls the default.

# Mission Control and Spaces on Mac

Mission Control is the bird's-eye view of every open window. Spaces
are macOS's virtual desktops.

## Opening Mission Control

* Three-finger swipe up on the trackpad, or
* Press the **Mission Control** key on the keyboard (looks like
  three rectangles), or
* Press **Control + Up Arrow**.

## Adding a new Space

In Mission Control, hover the top-right corner. A **+** button
appears. Click it to create a new desktop space.

## Switching Spaces

* Three-finger swipe left or right on the trackpad, or
* Press **Control + Left/Right Arrow**, or
* Open Mission Control and click a space at the top.

## Moving a window to another Space

* In Mission Control, drag a window's preview onto a space at the top.
* Or drag the window itself to the edge of the screen and hold —
  after a moment, the next Space slides in.

## Assigning an app to a specific Space

1. Right-click the app's icon in the Dock.
2. Choose **Options**.
3. Pick **All Desktops**, **This Desktop**, or **None**.

This is great for keeping Mail on Space 1, your work browser on
Space 2, and so on.

## Hot Corners

Hot Corners trigger Mission Control (or other actions) when you
move the mouse to a corner.

1. **System Settings → Desktop & Dock**.
2. Scroll to **Hot Corners…**.
3. Pick an action for each corner — Mission Control, Notification
   Center, Lock Screen, Sleep Display.

## Why Mission Control feels slow

Reduce animations under **System Settings → Accessibility → Display →
Reduce motion**. Mission Control transitions become a quick fade
instead of a swoop.

# Mission Control and Spaces on Mac

Mission Control is the bird's-eye view of every open window. Spaces
are macOS's virtual desktops.

## Opening Mission Control

* Three-finger swipe up on the trackpad, or
* Press the **Mission Control** key on the keyboard (looks like
  three rectangles), or
* Press **Control + Up Arrow**.

## Adding a new Space

In Mission Control, hover the top-right corner. A **+** button
appears. Click it to create a new desktop space.

## Switching Spaces

* Three-finger swipe left or right on the trackpad, or
* Press **Control + Left/Right Arrow**, or
* Open Mission Control and click a space at the top.

## Moving a window to another Space

* In Mission Control, drag a window's preview onto a space at the top.
* Or drag the window itself to the edge of the screen and hold —
  after a moment, the next Space slides in.

## Assigning an app to a specific Space

1. Right-click the app's icon in the Dock.
2. Choose **Options**.
3. Pick **All Desktops**, **This Desktop**, or **None**.

This is great for keeping Mail on Space 1, your work browser on
Space 2, and so on.

## Hot Corners

Hot Corners trigger Mission Control (or other actions) when you
move the mouse to a corner.

1. **System Settings → Desktop & Dock**.
2. Scroll to **Hot Corners…**.
3. Pick an action for each corner — Mission Control, Notification
   Center, Lock Screen, Sleep Display.

## Why Mission Control feels slow

Reduce animations under **System Settings → Accessibility → Display →
Reduce motion**. Mission Control transitions become a quick fade
instead of a swoop.

# Set the default web browser and email app on Mac

When you click a link, macOS opens it in the **default browser**.
When you click a `mailto:` link, macOS opens the **default email
client**.

## Default web browser

1. Open **System Settings → Desktop & Dock**.
2. Scroll to **Default web browser**.
3. Choose Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or any installed browser.

## Default email client

This setting lives inside the Mail app, not System Settings.

1. Open **Mail**.
2. Go to **Mail → Settings → General**.
3. Pick a different app from **Default email reader**.

## What happens when the default browser is uninstalled

If the default browser is no longer installed, macOS falls back to
**Safari**. Set a new default before uninstalling the previous one to
avoid surprises.

## Open links from a specific app in a different browser

Some apps offer their own per-app browser preference. For example,
the Slack desktop app has **Slack → Preferences → Advanced → Open all
links in a default browser**.

## Why a setting keeps reverting

A few apps re-prompt for default-browser status on every launch.

# Mission Control and Spaces on Mac

Mission Control is the bird's-eye view of every open window. Spaces
are macOS's virtual desktops.

## Opening Mission Control

* Three-finger swipe up on the trackpad, or
* Press the **Mission Control** key on the keyboard (looks like
  three rectangles), or
* Press **Control + Up Arrow**.

## Adding a new Space

In Mission Control, hover the top-right corner. A **+** button
appears. Click it to create a new desktop space.

## Switching Spaces

* Three-finger swipe left or right on the trackpad, or
* Press **Control + Left/Right Arrow**, or
* Open Mission Control and click a space at the top.

## Moving a window to another Space

* In Mission Control, drag a window's preview onto a space at the top.
* Or drag the window itself to the edge of the screen and hold —
  after a moment, the next Space slides in.

## Assigning an app to a specific Space

1. Right-click the app's icon in the Dock.
2. Choose **Options**.
3. Pick **All Desktops**, **This Desktop**, or **None**.

This is great for keeping Mail on Space 1, your work browser on
Space 2, and so on.

## Hot Corners

Hot Corners trigger Mission Control (or other actions) when you
move the mouse to a corner.

1. **System Settings → Desktop & Dock**.
2. Scroll to **Hot Corners…**.
3. Pick an action for each corner — Mission Control, Notification
   Center, Lock Screen, Sleep Display.

## Why Mission Control feels slow

Reduce animations under **System Settings → Accessibility → Display →
Reduce motion**. Mission Control transitions become a quick fade
instead of a swoop.
